options: Cellobiose as the only possible product
Free glucose only, with no phosphate
Glucose 1-phosphate
Fructose 1,6-bisphosphate
explanation: Phosphorolysis uses inorganic phosphate and releases glucose 1-phosphate from a suitable chain end. This is not the same as hydrolysis yielding a free sugar. The slide’s accompanying broad phrase must be interpreted with its explicitly labelled sugar-phosphate product.

question: Which statement correctly describes α-amylase in the stated comparison?
options: It can only release one free glucose at a time from a nonreducing end
Its endo action means it cleaves only from an exposed nonreducing terminus
It cleaves every α(1→6) branch and every β(1→4) cellulose link identically
It acts internally on suitable α(1→4) chains and leaves further processing necessary
explanation: Endo action on α(1→4) links produces shorter chains and products such as maltose/maltotriose. Branches and other linkages require appropriate additional activities. Endo/exo mode, linkage recognition and final absorbable products must be kept separate.

question: Why does iodine give a characteristic colour with suitable amylose preparations?
options: Any free glucose molecule gives the same iodine complex as an amylose helix
Iodine necessarily reduces copper(II) to copper(I)
All carbohydrate-containing samples have the same response
An amylose helix accommodates iodine/polyiodide species
explanation: The signal involves organisation of iodine-related species with a helical glucan structure. It is not a copper-reduction assay or a universal colour of individual glucose units. Chain conformation and assay conditions affect the response.

question: A starch–iodine colour disappears on heating. Why is a cooling comparison useful before claiming hydrolysis?
options: Heating can alter complex organisation without proving bond cleavage
Cooling automatically recreates all broken glycosidic bonds
Every heat-induced colour change proves conversion to pure glucose
A negative iodine colour proves absence of every carbohydrate
explanation: Temperature can change organisation of the colour complex, so colour loss alone does not establish cleavage. A cooling comparison and controlled digestion reference help distinguish mechanisms. Cooling is not assumed to reverse glycosidic hydrolysis or uniquely identify a product.

question: Which structural comparison explains why human α-amylase does not normally cleave cellulose?
options: Cellulose has β(1→4) glucose links rather than suitable α(1→4) links
Cellulose must contain a different monosaccharide because its digestibility differs
Cellulose differs from amylose only in chain length, not glycosidic configuration
All plant carbohydrate contains the same α linkage
explanation: Enzyme recognition depends on linkage geometry, not merely monomer identity. Cellulose and starch can both be glucose polymers while requiring different enzymes. Hydrogen bonding organises cellulose chains but does not replace their covalent glycosidic backbone.

question: Which pair correctly identifies the repeating sugars in bacterial peptidoglycan?
options: N-Acetylglucosamine and galactose with phosphate cross-links instead of peptides
Glucose and galactose without amino-sugar modification
N-Acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid
N-Acetylglucosamine alone, with no second alternating sugar or peptide connections
explanation: Peptidoglycan combines alternating modified sugars with peptide-associated cross-connections. It is neither an unmodified glucose storage glucan nor a nucleic-acid polymer. Exact peptide details vary among organisms, so the sugar pair is a more stable defining comparison.

question: Where is lipopolysaccharide located in the standard Gram-negative envelope comparison?
options: As an obligatory part of every Gram-positive plasma membrane
As an alternative name for the entire peptidoglycan layer
In the outer membrane as a lipid-associated glycoconjugate
As a free carbohydrate store in the bacterial cytosol
explanation: LPS is a distinct outer-membrane glycoconjugate with lipid A and carbohydrate regions. Peptidoglycan is a separate glycan–peptide network. The organism/envelope context matters; the comparison cannot be generalised to all bacteria or all cells.

question: Which residue name corrects the slide’s abbreviated galacturonan composition label?
options: Unmodified galactose only
Glycerol
Fructose 1-phosphate
Galacturonic acid/galacturonate
explanation: The uronan name identifies uronic-acid chemistry, including a carboxyl group. Galactan and galacturonan are therefore not interchangeable polymer names. Glycerol and fructose phosphate have different functional groups and backbones from the requested residue.

question: In the common N-linked protein-glycan context, which protein group participates?
options: Any arbitrary nitrogen in every peptide bond
Only a serine hydroxyl oxygen
A phosphate oxygen attached to glycogen
Asparagine side-chain amide nitrogen
explanation: N-linked glycosylation in this context specifies the asparagine side-chain amide attachment, whereas common O-linked attachment involves hydroxyl-bearing side chains. The labels identify a specific bond context rather than any occurrence of the element nitrogen.

question: Why do many GAG-rich extracellular matrices retain substantial water?
options: Their charged groups associate with counterions and water within an organised matrix
Their negative charge comes exclusively from the core protein rather than their sugar substituents
Their water retention follows solely from the total number of sugar carbons, regardless of charge
Every glycan retains the same amount of water regardless of charge and matrix organisation
explanation: Carboxylate and sulfate groups often confer negative charge and support hydration. Protein organisation and network interactions still contribute to mechanical behaviour. Hydration is not conversion of water into sugar or a property of nonpolar chains.

question: Which qualification prevents treating all GAGs as identically O-linked to core-protein serine?
options: Every visible association in a proteoglycan aggregate is a covalent bond
Hyaluronan lacks that ordinary covalent core attachment, and keratan sulfate has linkage variants
An N-linked keratan sulfate chain would contradict every possible proteoglycan structure
Hyaluronan must be covalently linked to core protein through the same serine linker as every sulfated GAG
explanation: Common linkage patterns have exceptions. Hyaluronan associates noncovalently with some proteoglycan systems, while keratan sulfate can have different N/O-linked contexts. A source generalisation should not erase those distinct architectures.

question: What is the defensible meaning of a positive Molisch carbohydrate screen?
options: Its exact glucose concentration is established
The sample is uniquely pure glucose
A carbohydrate-associated dehydration/condensation response is present under the test conditions
The sample contains no glycosidic bonds
explanation: Molisch is broad, involving furfural-related products and α-naphthol colour chemistry. A response does not uniquely identify a monosaccharide, establish purity or provide a calibrated concentration. The appropriate controls determine whether the observed interface can be interpreted.

question: Which test comparison uses orcinol and a pentose-derived furfural response?
options: A copper-specific Benedict reaction
The iodine–amylose helix test
Bial’s test
Seliwanoff’s test with resorcinol
explanation: Bial uses orcinol in acidic ferric-ion conditions to support a pentose comparison. Seliwanoff has a different aromatic reagent and kinetic ketose comparison, while Benedict and iodine detect different chemistry. Reagent and mechanism should be matched rather than memorising colour alone.

question: Why can prolonged Seliwanoff heating weaken a simple ketose-versus-aldose interpretation?
options: Ketoses cannot ever form coloured products
Colour formation measures only the initial carbonyl identity, independent of later reactions
A delayed colour uniquely identifies the original sample as free fructose
The discrimination depends on reaction rate and can be confounded by rearrangement or hydrolysis
explanation: The intended contrast is faster ketose colour under controlled conditions, not an absolute permanent colour prohibition for all other samples. Hydrolysable sucrose can supply fructose, and extended reactions can blur categories. A standardised comparison is needed.

question: A reagent blank develops the same unexpected colour as the unknown. What should happen to the interpretation?
options: Accept the unknown as definitively positive regardless
Investigate background/reagent validity before accepting the sample classification
Record a quantitative glucose concentration from colour alone
Conclude the unknown contains no carbohydrate with certainty
explanation: The blank reveals signal that does not depend on the unknown, so the run cannot support the intended sample conclusion without investigation. Neither an automatic positive nor an automatic negative follows. Controls establish interpretability rather than acting as optional decoration.

question: During a positive Benedict reducing-sugar reaction, which redox description is correct?
options: The sugar is oxidised while Cu²⁺ is reduced toward Cu⁺
The sugar and Cu²⁺ are both reduced
Cu⁺ is oxidised to Cu²⁺ to create the stated precipitate
The brick-red solid must be elemental copper
explanation: The sugar acts as the reducing agent and is itself oxidised; copper(II) is reduced to copper(I), commonly observed as Cu₂O. Oxidation of copper in the opposite direction or equating the precipitate with metallic copper misidentifies the reaction.

question: Why can fructose give a positive alkaline Benedict reaction despite being a ketose?
options: Benedict reagent is glucose-specific and cannot detect products arising from ketose rearrangement
Alkaline rearrangement can generate reactive aldose forms through enediol chemistry
Every ketose is permanently nonreducing
A ketose must contain a free aldehyde in its original structure to react under any conditions
explanation: The alkaline chemistry permits rearrangement, so the drawn ketone alone is not sufficient to predict a negative result. This is distinct from claiming all ketones under all conditions reduce copper. Structure must be considered with the actual assay environment.

question: A Barfoed precipitate appears only after prolonged heating. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The mono/disaccharide distinction is independent of heating duration and acid hydrolysis
The observation establishes an exact blood-glucose concentration
The original sample was certainly a pure monosaccharide
Slow disaccharide reaction or hydrolysis can confound the timed classification
explanation: Barfoed relies on a controlled rate contrast; the source itself allows slower disaccharide responses. A late positive cannot uniquely classify the starting sample. Concentration, conditions and references must be checked rather than applying an unlimited-time rule.

question: Why is an uncalibrated Benedict colour ladder insufficient for an exact glucose concentration?
options: The test directly distinguishes glucose from every other reducing substance
Colour intensity is independent of heating and sample composition
The illustrative colour categories alone provide a matrix-independent concentration
Colour depends on conditions, matrix and reducing substances, and the assay is not uniquely glucose-specific
explanation: The signal is influenced by preparation and multiple reducing components. A validated calibration and appropriate sample context are required for quantitative interpretation; the lecture illustration alone is not a measurement made on the unknown.

question: The unknown is negative but the known positive control also fails to react. Which result should be recorded?
options: A certified absence of every carbohydrate
An inconclusive run requiring investigation or repeat under valid conditions
A valid negative classification because reagent performance does not affect negative samples
A conclusive negative because matching the failed positive control validates the unknown
explanation: A failed positive control does not demonstrate that the reagent/procedure could detect the intended target. The unknown’s negative response is therefore not reliable evidence of absence. Matching colours cannot replace proof of assay performance.

question: Which pair contains the canonical purine bases?
options: Adenine and guanine
Cytosine and thymine
Uracil and cytosine
Adenine and thymine
explanation: Adenine and guanine have the fused purine ring system. Cytosine, thymine and uracil are pyrimidines. Ring classification is distinct from whether a base is attached to sugar or phosphate.

question: A molecule contains adenine and ribose but no phosphate. Which description fits?
options: dAMP, a deoxynucleotide
Adenosine, a nucleoside
AMP, a nucleotide
Adenine alone, a free base
explanation: Base plus ribose gives adenosine; phosphate is needed for AMP, and deoxy forms use a different sugar. Removing or adding phosphate does not by itself specify a change in base identity.

question: Which canonical linkage joins the sugar to a purine base?
options: Sugar C3′ to base C6
Sugar C2′ to base N9
Sugar C1′ to base N9
Sugar C5′ to base N1
explanation: The canonical β N-glycosidic linkage uses sugar C1′ and purine N9; pyrimidines usually use N1 instead. Prime marks identify sugar positions and must not be confused with base-ring numbers.

question: Which structural description distinguishes thymine from uracil?
options: Thymine is a two-ring purine whereas uracil is a pyrimidine
Thymine differs solely by replacement of ribose with deoxyribose in the free base
Thymine has one more phosphate in its base ring
Thymine is 5-methyluracil
explanation: The distinction is a methyl substitution at base C5, not a sugar or phosphate change. Both are pyrimidines. The usual DNA/RNA distribution is a separate biological context and has modified-RNA qualifications.

question: Which statement correctly uses prime numbering?
options: C1′ identifies a sugar atom, while N1 identifies an unprimed base atom
C1′ and N1 must be the same atom in a pyrimidine nucleoside
All primed positions belong to the phosphate chain
The prime mark specifies the base’s optical rotation
explanation: Prime marks separate the pentose numbering from base-ring numbering. They do not identify charge or rotation. A sugar C1′–base N1 linkage connects two distinct atoms rather than giving one atom two interchangeable labels.

question: Which charge statement is appropriate for the ordinary internal phosphodiester backbone near physiological pH?
options: Approximately one negative charge per internal phosphate, with context-dependent ionisation
Exactly two positive charges per phosphate at every pH
A mandatory minus-two per link identical to every free monoester
A completely uncharged backbone because each strand pairs with another
explanation: Phosphodiester and phosphate-monoester ionisation patterns differ. Pairing does not neutralise each backbone phosphate, and pH/counterion context must be retained. The source’s broad doubly-ionised statement cannot simply be multiplied across every polymer link.

question: Why is isolated bond breaking insufficient to explain ATP hydrolysis free energy?
options: ATP can drive any nearby reaction without a coupling mechanism
Bond cleavage requires energy; net favourability depends on the whole reaction and conditions
Breaking any chemical bond necessarily releases its entire formation energy
Product hydration and concentration cannot affect reaction free energy
explanation: The overall reaction includes bond changes, product stabilisation, solvation, ionisation and concentrations. Coupling requires a molecular connection, not proximity alone. Energy-rich bond is useful shorthand only if that whole-reaction context is preserved.

question: Which assignment separates nucleotide-derived cellular roles correctly?
options: CoA as the redox cofactor in every pathway and NAD as the carrier of every acyl group
NAD and FAD as identical cofactors that cannot differ in their electron-transfer chemistry
cAMP signalling, NAD/FAD redox-related cofactors and CoA acyl transfer
cAMP as an acyl carrier, NAD/FAD as structural DNA sugars and CoA as a coding triplet
explanation: These derivatives support different functions and molecular structures. Sharing nucleotide-related chemistry does not make them identical or assign every role to ATP. The specific transported group or signal matters.

question: Does one free nucleotide automatically have the catalytic function of a ribozyme containing that residue?
options: Yes; every RNA monomer alone performs the complete ribozyme reaction
Yes; any phosphate-containing polymer has the same catalytic activity as every ribozyme
No; RNA can never catalyse a biological reaction
No; catalytic function depends on organised sequence, folding and chemical context
explanation: A building unit is not equivalent to the assembled catalyst. Ribozymes depend on molecular organisation and can involve ions and specific groups. Rejecting automatic monomer catalysis does not deny RNA catalysis itself.

question: Which connection is the ordinary covalent backbone link between successive nucleic-acid sugars?
options: N9–N1 hydrogen bond
C1′–base glycosidic bond repeated between every sugar
A peptide bond between base amino groups
3′–5′ phosphodiester
explanation: The bridge connects sugar 3′ oxygen through phosphate to the next sugar’s 5′ oxygen. The sugar–base glycosidic bond and interstrand pairing are different structural connections. Ordinary nucleic-acid backbones are not peptide chains.

question: What is the complementary DNA strand to 5′-AGTC-3′ when also written 5′→3′?
options: 5′-GACT-3′
5′-TCAG-3′
5′-AGTC-3′
5′-CTGA-3′
explanation: Directly opposite is 3′-TCAG-5′; reverse its written order to report 5′-GACT-3′. Merely substituting complementary bases without reversing orientation gives the common TCAG error. The two backbones run antiparallel.

question: How many internal phosphodiester links occur in two separate linear five-nucleotide strands?
options: Twenty
Eight
Ten
Five
explanation: Each linear five-residue strand has four internal links, so the two have eight. A covalently closed circle would change that count, while base-pair hydrogen bonds do not add internal backbone links. Terminal phosphorylation is another distinct feature.

question: For four independently chosen oriented DNA positions with four canonical letters, how many sequence strings are possible?
explanation: The stated model gives 4⁴=256. Specifying a canonical complementary strand does not add another independent sequence choice for every paired position. This count concerns a defined orientation and length rather than literally infinite information.

question: Which group normally supports the next polymerase-mediated extension of a growing nucleic-acid strand?
options: An arbitrary base methyl group
A required free 2′ OH on every DNA residue
The complete retention of each incoming triphosphate as three internal backbone links
The growing 3′ OH
explanation: Standard extension uses the growing strand’s 3′ OH with an incoming nucleotide triphosphate. DNA lacks 2′ OH but can still extend. Incorporation releases pyrophosphate rather than retaining three separate internal links per residue.

question: If adenine is 30% of all bases in a fully paired canonical DNA duplex, what is cytosine’s percentage?
explanation: A=T gives 60% combined, leaving 40% G+C; equal G and C therefore contribute 20% each. The denominator includes both strands, and the result depends on the canonical duplex assumption.

question: A 1,000-base-pair canonical duplex has 40% GC pairs. How many total nucleotide residues does it contain?
explanation: Each base pair contains two nucleotide residues, giving 2,000 in the duplex. The 400 value is its GC-pair count and 2,400 can be the ideal hydrogen-bond count for this particular composition, not the residue total.

question: Using three hydrogen bonds per GC pair and two per AT pair, what ideal count follows for 400 GC and 600 AT pairs?
explanation: Compute 400×3+600×2=2,400. This is an ideal interbase hydrogen-bond count under the supplied model, not a count of nucleotide residues, phosphodiester links or a complete free-energy calculation.

question: When can the whole-molecule A=T and G=C equalities be applied as taught here?
options: To every single-stranded cellular RNA using T rather than U
Only if all four bases are present at exactly 25% each
To the complete ordinary canonically paired DNA duplex
To every isolated DNA strand regardless of its partner
explanation: Canonical pairing imposes the equality across both strands together. An individual strand need not satisfy it, and single-stranded RNA has no corresponding universal composition equality. Pairing assumptions and the counted molecule must be specified.

question: Two fragments have the same GC percentage. What does that alone establish?
options: Identical base order at every position
Identical melting temperature under all solvent and salt conditions
The absence of every possible mismatch
A shared aggregate composition measure, not an identical sequence or guaranteed identical Tm
explanation: Composition does not specify sequence order, and Tm also depends on length, context and solution conditions. Equal GC percentages therefore cannot certify molecular identity or every duplex property.

question: Which description correctly contrasts common DNA helix forms?
options: All three are identical right-handed helices with different base alphabets
B is left-handed and Z right-handed
A/B/Z labels directly specify phosphate charge signs
A and B are right-handed; Z is left-handed in its characteristic context
explanation: The forms differ in geometry and conditions rather than base alphabet or a switch in backbone charge. Local conformation must be distinguished from global supercoiling. The labels do not imply that each form occurs equally in every sequence.

question: What does supercoiling describe most directly?
options: The path of the duplex axis in space
The pitch of one local helical turn considered independently of the larger-scale duplex axis
A change in sequence composition with no change to the duplex axis path
The 5′→3′ direction of a single strand rather than the spatial arrangement of the duplex axis
explanation: Supercoiling concerns larger-scale organisation of the duplex axis, distinct from local helix form or chemical degradation. Covalent topology constrains the possible configurations in closed DNA. A change in shape is not automatically a change in chemical alphabet.

question: Which statement correctly describes the nucleosome core comparison?
options: Exactly 147 nucleotides total across both strands including all linker DNA
A histone octamer with about 147 wrapped base pairs; H1 is a distinct linker-associated histone
A nine-member core octamer that includes H1
A core in which linker H1 replaces the H2A–H2B pairs of the ordinary octamer
explanation: The approximate core wrap is 147 base pairs, not 147 total residues or a universal linker-inclusive repeat. H1 is not part of the eight core histone copies. Packaging involves a DNA–protein assembly while its boundaries and context must be specified.

question: Why is one extra GC hydrogen bond not a complete explanation of duplex stability?
options: Every AT-rich sequence is necessarily more stable under every condition
Solvent and ionic conditions are irrelevant once the canonical base pairs are specified
Base stacking, solvent, ions, sequence and conditions also contribute
Hydrogen bonds are the covalent bonds forming each sugar–phosphate link
explanation: Base pairing supports specificity, but stability is a whole-system property involving multiple interactions and conditions. A bond count alone does not provide the full free-energy comparison. This qualification does not deny canonical hydrogen bonding.

question: A sample has A260=.90 and A280=.50. What ratio follows?
explanation: Divide .90 by .50 to obtain 1.8. That value can be compared with the stated screening guide, but by itself does not establish integrity, complete purity or successful downstream function.

question: A blank-corrected 1:20 sample has A260=.20. With an explicitly supplied factor of 50 µg/mL per unit at the calibration path length, what original concentration is calculated?
options: 10 µg/mL
0.5 µg/mL
1,000 µg/mL
200 µg/mL
explanation: The diluted concentration is .20×50=10 µg/mL; multiply by the twenty-fold dilution to recover 200 µg/mL. The factor applies to the stated molecule/path calibration, not all nucleic-acid samples. Dividing by dilution reverses the needed correction.

question: A260 rises from .50 to .70 in an illustrative denaturation example. What is the relative increase?
explanation: The change is .20 relative to the original .50: .20/.50×100=40%. The absolute absorbance difference is not itself the percent change, and the high plateau is not the denominator for this stated relative increase.

question: An illustrative melting signal has plateaus .50 and .70 and reaches .60 at 70°C. Which operational Tm follows?
options: 40°C solely because the signal increases by 40%
70°C, at half of the baseline-corrected signal change
The temperature at A260=.35, half the high plateau
The first temperature at which any base pair opens
explanation: Half the .20 signal change lies .10 above the low plateau, at .60. The supplied curve reaches that signal at 70°C. Tm is not determined by half of the raw upper reading or by percent increase alone.

question: What does an A260/A280 ratio near the DNA reference guide fail to prove on its own?
options: That nucleic acids can absorb near 260 nm
That the measurement may contribute to a purity screen
That the DNA is intact and suitable for every downstream assay
That a ratio can be calculated from two absorbances
explanation: A suitable-looking ratio can coexist with fragmentation or other quality problems. Integrity and downstream performance need additional evidence, while blank, pH and concentration also affect interpretation. The ratio remains useful as a screen within those limits.

question: Which RNA group enables the neighbouring-group alkaline cleavage pathway?
options: A base amino group that replaces the leaving backbone oxygen at every RNA linkage
A terminal 5′ phosphate required to attack every internal linkage independently of the 2′ position
The 2′ OH after deprotonation
A required 2′ OH present in every DNA sugar
explanation: RNA’s 2′ oxygen can become nucleophilic and attack the neighbouring phosphate. DNA lacks that 2′ OH and therefore this particular mechanism. The comparison concerns a chemical pathway, not universal resistance of DNA to every kind of damage.

question: Which intermediate/product pattern fits the stated RNA cleavage mechanism?
options: Two fragments each required to retain the original intact 3′–5′ link across the cleavage site
Only cleavage of the base–sugar bond, leaving every phosphodiester unchanged
Only loss of hydrogen bonds with no covalent change
A 2′,3′-cyclic phosphate on one fragment and a 5′ OH on the other
explanation: Intramolecular attack can cleave the backbone through a cyclic phosphate, with a departing 5′-OH fragment. Further hydrolysis opens that cyclic phosphate. This is covalent cleavage, unlike simple duplex denaturation.

question: What can initially result from depurination without immediate backbone scission?
options: An abasic site after cleavage of the sugar–purine glycosidic bond
A phosphodiester break that leaves the purine–sugar bond unchanged
Only thermal strand separation, with no change in the sugar–base bond
Deamination of the base while its sugar linkage remains unchanged
explanation: Depurination removes the base through its sugar linkage and can leave the sugar–phosphate chain initially continuous. It differs from phosphodiester hydrolysis, translation or a universal sugar conversion. Subsequent damage processing is a separate issue.

question: Which conclusion correctly qualifies DNA’s resistance to RNA-type alkaline cleavage?
options: Every RNA in every protected cellular complex must degrade faster than all DNA
It lacks that 2′-OH pathway but remains susceptible to other damage mechanisms
It cannot mutate under any chemical or biological conditions
It lacks all hydroxyl groups at every sugar position
explanation: A specific structural difference explains a specific relative susceptibility. DNA can still undergo acid-related, oxidative, enzymatic or other damage, while cellular RNA stability depends on its context. The source’s stable-archive comparison cannot establish absolute immunity.

question: For mRNA codon 5′-AUG-3′, which simple complementary anticodon is written 5′→3′?
options: GUA
CAU
UAC
AUG
explanation: The aligned partner is 3′-UAC-5′; reversing its written direction gives 5′-CAU-3′. The orientation step is essential. Wobble can complicate real decoding, but this question explicitly uses simple Watson–Crick complementarity.

question: Which task is distinct from codon–anticodon pairing and is performed in charging tRNA?
options: Replacing an anticodon with an amino-acid sequence during charging
Joining the amino acid to the tRNA’s 5′ end as the obligatory standard attachment site
Attaching the appropriate amino acid with an aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase
Attaching an amino acid solely through codon pairing, without a charging enzyme
explanation: A synthetase helps link the appropriate amino acid to tRNA, whereas pairing recognises the mRNA triplet at the ribosome. Decoding alone does not chemically charge the adaptor. The two activities connect but are not interchangeable.

question: Which statement correctly describes the ribosomal catalytic example?
options: The whole ribosome lacks proteins because rRNA has a catalytic role
Every rRNA molecule contains the same exact length in every organism
mRNA is the structural core that directly replaces all large-subunit rRNA
The peptidyl-transferase centre is RNA-based within a ribonucleoprotein assembly
explanation: RNA-based catalysis is compatible with important ribosomal proteins and organism-specific assembly. A catalytic-centre assignment does not imply a protein-free ribosome or universal inventory. Distinguish the catalytic component from the entire complex.

question: A 12-nucleotide segment starts at a defined coding-frame boundary. What can be said before inspecting whether any triplet is a stop?
options: It contains four complete triplets, but not necessarily four encoded amino acids
It must encode twelve amino acids
It has only three complete triplets
Every triplet must be a start codon
explanation: Twelve divided by three gives four triplets. Stop codons and biological context determine how many amino acids are produced; triplet count alone is insufficient. The reading-frame boundary is explicitly specified to avoid an offset ambiguity.

question: Which comparison assigns snRNA and tRNA roles appropriately?
options: snRNA-associated processing/splicing versus tRNA adaptor function in translation
snRNA carrying every amino acid while tRNA removes all introns
Both are obligatory protein-coding messages whose functions arise only after translation
Both must be protein-coding mRNAs because they have functions
explanation: snRNAs participate in RNA-processing assemblies; tRNA connects codon recognition with amino-acid delivery. Functional RNA need not be translated. The activities differ even though both can involve structured RNA and protein partners.

question: Does classifying a transcript as noncoding establish that it is useless?
options: Yes; only mRNA can contribute to gene expression
No; many essential RNAs function without translation, but a specific transcript’s role still needs evidence
Yes; all untranslatable RNA is necessarily nonfunctional
No; it proves every observed transcript has one identical regulatory role
explanation: Noncoding describes protein-coding status in the role considered, not absence of molecular activity. rRNA and tRNA are essential examples. However, a label alone does not experimentally establish the function of every particular transcript.

question: Why should sRNA be interpreted using context rather than as one universal molecular class?
options: It fixes a universal size boundary shared by every historical use of the term
It unambiguously identifies amino-acid-carrying tRNA in every modern small-RNA context
The abbreviation has been used for soluble tRNA and for small-RNA contexts with different roles
It always identifies one identical mechanism in bacterial small RNAs and historical soluble RNA
explanation: Historical soluble-RNA usage and modern small-RNA terminology are not identical definitions. Role, organism and evidence clarify the intended meaning. An abbreviation alone supplies neither a universal length nor a coding-status conclusion.

question: Which activation step is important to the zidovudine mechanism taught here?
options: Oxidation into urate as the required active polymerase substrate
Addition of a normal 3′ OH that creates an ordinary thymidine substrate
Intracellular phosphorylation to the active triphosphate
Loss of its thymine ring before use as the ordinary deoxyribonucleotide substrate
explanation: The nucleoside analogue is phosphorylated intracellularly. Its active form can be incorporated in the reverse-transcriptase-related pathway and terminate extension because the ordinary 3′ OH is absent. Structural form and activation matter; this is not a dosing recommendation.

question: Why should 5-fluorouracil not be described only as an ordinary 3′-deoxy chain terminator?
options: Its parent base already contains the same 3′-azido sugar substitution as zidovudine
Its phosphate-free parent is directly incorporated unchanged as a complete DNA nucleotide
Every analogue necessarily has the same activation pathway and target
Its active metabolites have distinct actions, including FdUMP inhibition of thymidylate synthase
explanation: The fluoropyrimidine base analogue has multiple metabolic mechanisms, including altered nucleotide supply and RNA/DNA effects. It is not equivalent to every sugar-modified nucleoside analogue. Chemical similarity does not erase differences in active form or target.

question: Which sequence correctly follows the source-linked purine product comparison?
options: Hypoxanthine can be oxidised to xanthine and then urate
Urate is normally converted by functional human uricase in every cell
Guanine deamination bypasses xanthine and directly yields hypoxanthine
Every elevated urate value by itself diagnoses gout
explanation: The linked oxidation sequence differs from guanine deamination entering at xanthine. Humans lack functional uricase, and a metabolite measurement alone is not the same as crystal-associated inflammatory disease. Biochemical pathways and diagnosis have different evidence requirements.

question: What can be concluded from finding a chemically modified base?
options: Every modification has the same effect as a therapeutic chain terminator
Its effect depends on the modification and context; it is not automatically a mutation or harmful lesion
It must always indicate an irreversible DNA sequence substitution
It necessarily breaks the phosphodiester backbone at that base position
explanation: Regulated base modifications and damaged bases both exist, with different biological consequences. The chemical identity, location and functional evidence are needed. A modification label alone cannot assign mutation, pathology or a drug mechanism.

question: Using the stated standard mRNA code table, which amino acid is specified by 5′-UGG-3′?
options: Tryptophan (Trp)
Cysteine (Cys)
A stop signal
Tyrosine (Tyr)
explanation: Select first base U, second G and third G: UGG specifies tryptophan in the standard code. UGU/UGC specify cysteine, UGA is a stop and UAU/UAC specify tyrosine. The third position and stated code context matter.

question: UUU and UUC both specify phenylalanine in the standard code. What does this illustrate?
options: Ambiguity: one codon randomly specifies different amino acids
A requirement that all three bases be identical for translation
Evidence that the two codons are different reading directions of one triplet
Degeneracy: more than one codon can specify the same amino acid
explanation: Degeneracy describes multiple codons assigned to one amino acid. It does not make the assignment of a given standard codon random or remove reading direction. The distinct third bases preserve the same phenylalanine assignment in this comparison.

question: Which description correctly distinguishes an ordinary internal residue from its free amino acid?
options: Its α-amino and α-carboxyl-derived groups usually participate in backbone amide linkages.
Its side chain must lose every ionisable group.
Its α carbon becomes a carbonyl carbon.
It retains an independent free α-amino and α-carboxyl pair at each position.
explanation: Incorporation creates backbone amides, so internal residues are not independent free zwitterions. Side-chain ionisable groups can remain; the α carbon remains distinct from the carbonyl carbon. Free terminal groups must be counted at chain ends rather than assigned to every residue.

question: Why is glycine achiral at its α carbon?
options: Its side chain contains a second stereocentre.
The α carbon has two identical hydrogen substituents.
Its carboxyl group has no oxygen.
Its amino nitrogen is part of a ring.
explanation: Glycine has R=H, giving two identical α-carbon substituents and no stereocentre there. It still has the ordinary carboxyl group. A ring joining the side chain to amino nitrogen describes proline, while a second side-chain stereocentre occurs in isoleucine and threonine.

question: Which description of free proline corrects a common structural misconception?
options: It has an ordinary primary amino group and an achiral α carbon.
Its sulfur atom directly forms the side-chain ring.
It contains a secondary amino group within a ring and retains its carboxyl group.
It lacks both an amino nitrogen and a carboxyl group.
explanation: Proline reconnects its side chain to the amino nitrogen, making a secondary amine and restricting geometry. The carboxyl remains present and its α carbon is chiral. Sulfur does not form this ring; cysteine and methionine are the common sulfur-containing residues.

question: What follows from assigning L configuration to a common chiral α-amino acid?
options: The sample must rotate plane-polarised light to the left.
The absolute configuration must be S in every case.
The molecule must have only one stereocentre.
A reference configuration is specified; measured optical rotation still needs independent information.
explanation: L/D is a configurational convention rather than a sign of optical rotation. L-cysteine illustrates why L does not universally equal S: sulfur changes the priority order. Isoleucine and threonine also show that an L amino acid can contain an additional stereocentre.

question: Which pair has side-chain carboxylates that are usually negatively charged near pH 7?
options: Aspartate and glutamate
Asparagine and glutamine
Lysine and arginine
Serine and threonine
explanation: Aspartate and glutamate have side-chain acid groups commonly deprotonated at neutral pH. Asparagine/glutamine have uncharged amides, lysine/arginine are usually positively charged, and serine/threonine have ordinarily uncharged hydroxyl side chains.

question: Which common sulfur residue supplies a thiol that can form an ordinary protein disulfide?
options: Asparagine
Cysteine
Methionine
Tyrosine
explanation: Two appropriate cysteine thiols can be oxidised into a disulfide. Methionine contains a thioether rather than that thiol. Tyrosine has a phenol and asparagine a carboxamide; neither provides the ordinary cysteine–cysteine disulfide chemistry.

question: Why is a basic classification insufficient to claim every histidine side chain is positive at pH 7?
options: Histidine has the same permanently charged group as arginine.
The side chain becomes a carboxylate at neutral pH.
Imidazole protonation depends on its pKa and environment; a substantial uncharged population can exist.
Basic residues cannot accept protons.
explanation: Histidine can accept or donate a proton, but its charged fraction depends on pH relative to its environment-dependent pKa. It is not permanently charged and does not acquire a carboxylate by ionisation. This equilibrium flexibility helps explain catalytic roles.

question: A surface glutamate is replaced by glutamine. Which chemical change is most directly expected near neutral pH?
options: A nonpolar hydrocarbon replaces the entire polar side chain.
A second positive guanidinium group is added.
A thiol becomes an interchain disulfide.
A similarly sized polar side chain loses the usual negative carboxylate charge.
explanation: Glutamine has a side-chain amide instead of glutamate’s carboxylate, retaining polarity while removing the usual negative charge. Valine would provide a more hydrocarbon-rich replacement; arginine supplies guanidinium and cysteine supplies a thiol. The functional effect still depends on location.

question: Which residue-code pairing is correct?
options: Tryptophan — Trp — W
Tyrosine — Trp — T
Threonine — Tyr — Y
Glutamine — Glu — E
explanation: Tryptophan is Trp/W. Tyrosine is Tyr/Y, threonine Thr/T and glutamine Gln/Q; Glu/E denotes glutamate. Correct code interpretation prevents reading a different chemical side chain into a sequence.

question: For one acid–base pair at pH equal to its pKa, what concentration relationship follows?
options: The whole protein must be at its isoelectric point.
Deprotonated and protonated forms have equal concentrations.
Only the protonated form can be present.
The deprotonated form is ten times as abundant.
explanation: Henderson–Hasselbalch gives log10(base/acid)=0, so the ratio is one. A 10:1 ratio requires pH one unit above pKa. Equality for one group does not establish zero net charge for a molecule with other ionisable groups.

question: A supplied two-group example has pKa values 2.4 and 9.6, with the net-zero state between them. What pI follows in the ideal model?
explanation: The two dissociations bracketing the zero-charge state give pI=(2.4+9.6)/2=6.0. The lower pKa alone is one group’s midpoint, the pKa difference 7.2 is not the pI, and the unaveraged sum 12.0 omits division by two.

question: For a lysine-like example, successive supplied pKa values are 2.2, 9.0 and 10.5 and charges change +2→+1→0→−1. What pI follows?
explanation: The zero state is between the dissociations at 9.0 and 10.5, giving (9.0+10.5)/2=9.75. Averaging the first two gives 5.60, the first and last 6.35 and all three about 7.23; none brackets the stated zero-charge state.

question: An aspartate-like example has supplied pKa values 2.0, 3.9 and 9.9 and charges +1→0→−1→−2. What is its ideal pI?
explanation: Here the neutral state lies between the first two dissociations, so pI=(2.0+3.9)/2=2.95. Using the first and last or last two averages the wrong states, while averaging all three ignores which forms bracket zero.

question: Using a supplied ammonium pKa of 9.6 at pH 8.6, approximately what fraction remains protonated in a simple single-group model?
explanation: Deprotonated/protonated=10^(8.6−9.6)=0.1. The protonated fraction is 1/(1+0.1)=0.909, about 91%. Nine percent is approximately the opposite fraction; 50% belongs at pH=pKa and 99% would require about two pH units below pKa.

question: With a supplied histidine side-chain pKa of 6.0 at pH 7.0, approximately what fraction is positively charged in the simple model?
explanation: The neutral/protonated ratio is 10^(7−6)=10, so the protonated positive fraction is 1/(1+10)=1/11≈9.1%. The inverse fraction is 90.9%; 50% occurs at pKa, and 1% would be closer to two pH units above pKa.

question: At a protein’s pI, which statement is justified?
options: Every side chain has lost its formal charge.
Every protein must precipitate completely.
Its pI equals the mean of its free amino-acid pIs.
Its population has zero average net charge, although charged groups can remain.
explanation: pI concerns the sum of charge contributions, not disappearance of all charged groups. Reduced repulsion can favour lower solubility, but precipitation depends on the protein and solution. Protein pI is not obtained by simply averaging the pIs of free amino acids.

question: Which classification should replace a general adult-human claim that histidine is merely semi-essential?
options: Histidine is one of the nine routinely indispensable amino acids.
Histidine is a dispensable carbohydrate.
Histidine is never used in proteins.
Histidine and arginine are permanently interchangeable dietary categories.
explanation: Human indispensability includes histidine. Arginine may be conditionally indispensable, so the two should not be assigned an identical universal category. Histidine remains an amino acid with important structural and catalytic roles; dietary classification does not remove it from proteins.

question: Why can abundant dietary amounts of other amino acids fail to compensate directly for one limiting indispensable amino acid during synthesis of a specified protein?
options: Protein synthesis depends only on total amino-acid mass.
The required residue must occupy its specified sequence positions and cannot simply be replaced by any abundant residue.
Any side chain becomes the missing amino acid through peptide-bond formation.
Transamination creates every missing carbon skeleton without a pathway.
explanation: A defined protein sequence requires particular residue identities. Total mass alone does not ensure a suitable amino-acid pattern. Transamination needs an appropriate skeleton and enzymes, and peptide formation does not transform arbitrary side chains into the required one. Overall nutrition remains more complex than this single limitation.

question: Which statement correctly distinguishes two post-translational modifications?
options: Every phosphorylation event activates every enzyme.
A hydroxyproline residue must be inserted by a separate ordinary hydroxyproline codon.
Lysine acetylation can neutralise its usual positive ε-amino charge, while phosphorylation adds a chemically different phosphate group.
Acetylation and phosphorylation are two names for the same group.
explanation: Acetyl and phosphate additions have different structures and effects. Phosphorylation can activate, inhibit or change recognition depending on the protein. Collagen hydroxylation modifies incorporated residues rather than requiring the asserted separate ordinary codon assignment.

question: Which precursor-to-product description is correct?
options: Histidine is a standard protein residue named adrenaline after folding.
Thyroglobulin is itself the free T3 hormone.
β-Alanine has its amino group on the same carbon as an α-amino acid.
Glutamate can be decarboxylated to GABA.
explanation: Glutamate decarboxylation removes CO2 to form GABA. Adrenaline derives from tyrosine through a pathway, not from renaming histidine. T3 is released after modification and processing of thyroglobulin; β-alanine differs in amino-group position from an α-amino acid.

question: What distinguishes an acid–base salt formation between amino-acid groups from a peptide-forming reaction?
options: Proton transfer alone does not create the new covalent carbonyl C–N amide linkage.
Both processes necessarily cleave the same backbone bond.
Salt formation always consumes activated aminoacyl-tRNA.
Any aqueous amino-acid mixture spontaneously becomes a protein.
explanation: Acid–base exchange changes protonation and ionic association, whereas peptide formation changes covalent connectivity and requires appropriate chemistry. Activated tRNA is part of cellular peptide synthesis, not a requirement for ordinary salt formation. Mixing free amino acids does not supply a complete spontaneous protein-synthesis pathway.

question: Which outcome is expected for free proline in the ordinary ninhydrin test rather than assuming a uniform purple response?
options: A specific red signal proving a peptide sequence
A different yellow product associated with its secondary amino group
The identical purple response of every primary α-amino acid at equal intensity
No possible reaction because proline has no nitrogen
explanation: Proline’s secondary amino chemistry gives a yellow product under ordinary test conditions. It does contain nitrogen. Neither its colour nor a purple response uniquely proves sequence, and equal molar response cannot be assumed across all analytes.

question: Which statement correctly separates UV and ordinary mid-infrared absorption?
options: Both are identical measurements of peptide sequence.
Infrared excites the same electronic transitions as UV in every amino acid.
UV commonly probes electronic transitions; mid-infrared commonly probes molecular vibrations.
Both necessarily involve only nuclear decay.
explanation: UV and infrared have different energy regimes and common transition types. Mid-infrared stretching and bending differ from the electronic excitations relevant to UV absorption. Neither measurement alone reads the complete residue sequence, and ordinary absorption is not nuclear decay.

question: Aromatic amino-acid spectra have all been normalised to equal maximum height. What comparison is unsafe from that plot alone?
options: Their peak wavelengths differ.
Their rescaled spectral shapes can be compared.
A curve extends over a different wavelength region.
Their absolute molar absorptivities are equal because the plotted peaks are equal.
explanation: Normalisation removes the original absolute amplitude scale, so equal plotted peaks cannot establish equal molar absorptivity. Wavelength positions and normalised shapes remain interpretable. Concentration estimates require an appropriate absolute calibration rather than a rescaled drawing.

question: For a theoretical protein, A280=0.50, ε=10,000 L mol−1 cm−1 and path length=1 cm. The measured solution is a tenfold dilution. What original concentration follows?
options: 500 µmol/L
50 µmol/L
5 µmol/L
5,000 µmol/L
explanation: A=εcl gives measured c=0.50/10,000=5×10−5 mol/L=50 µmol/L. Multiplying by ten gives the original 500 µmol/L. Fifty omits dilution correction, five reverses it and 5,000 adds an extra factor of ten. The supplied model assumes suitable blank correction and linearity.

question: For an unmodified ordinary linear peptide, what establishes the written sequence direction?
options: It runs from a β-sheet subunit to an α-helical subunit.
The sequence runs from its N terminus towards its C terminus.
It runs from the most hydrophobic residue towards the least hydrophobic.
It is determined by the left-to-right layout of any arbitrary sketch.
explanation: The sequence convention is N→C, independent of how a drawing is rotated or how hydrophobic the ends are. Secondary structures and chain-type labels do not define sequence direction. Terminal modifications require explicit description but do not reverse the standard notation.

question: Why is formal loss of water from two free amino acids an incomplete account of ribosomal peptide synthesis?
options: The ribosome directly joins adjacent α carbons.
Cellular synthesis occurs without chemical activation whenever free amino acids meet.
Cells use activated aminoacyl/peptidyl-tRNA chemistry and energy-dependent preparation.
Ribosomes join amino acids by a permanent salt interaction only.
explanation: A condensation balance tracks net atoms, but cellular synthesis uses activated tRNA-linked substrates prepared with ATP-derived energy. The new linkage is an amide between carbonyl carbon and nitrogen, not an α-carbon bond or a mere ionic salt. Encounter in water alone is insufficient.

question: Why is rotation about the peptide C–N bond restricted relative to adjacent backbone single bonds?
options: Each amino acid loses its carbonyl oxygen.
A peptide chain contains no single bonds anywhere.
The whole folded protein must lie in one geometric plane.
Resonance gives the amide C–N connection partial double-bond character.
explanation: Delocalisation within the amide favours a relatively planar peptide unit with restricted C–N rotation. Adjacent φ/ψ bonds still permit conformational variation within steric constraints. Carbonyl oxygen is retained, and local planarity does not make an entire protein planar.

question: Which statement correctly describes peptide geometry around proline?
options: Cis peptide units are relatively more frequent before proline, but a proline-containing bond is not automatically cis.
Every peptide unit before proline must be trans with no exceptions.
Every peptide unit before proline must be cis.
Proline supplies an extra internal peptide N–H donor.
explanation: The cis/trans balance is distinctive near proline, but neither conformation is a universal requirement for every such linkage. Internal proline lacks the ordinary N–H donor; it does not add one. Geometry and donor availability are separate effects.

question: How many backbone peptide bonds are present in ordinary linear Gly–Ala–Ser?
options: Four
Two
One
Three
explanation: A linear chain of three residues has n−1=2 backbone peptide bonds, one free N terminus and one free C terminus before modifications. Counting residues instead of connections gives three; counting termini as additional peptide bonds gives the other incorrect totals.

question: Separate unmodified linear chains contain 21 and 30 residues and are joined by disulfides. How many backbone peptide bonds are present?
explanation: Each chain contributes one fewer peptide bond than residues: 20+29=49. Treating the 51 residues as one chain gives 50 incorrectly. Disulfides join cysteine side chains and do not add backbone amides; their number must not be subtracted from the ordinary backbone count.

question: Using supplied free amino-acid masses Gly=75, Ala=89, Ser=105 and water=18 g/mol, what is the formal mass of ordinary linear Gly–Ala–Ser?
options: 269 g/mol
251 g/mol
215 g/mol
233 g/mol
explanation: The free-amino-acid total is 269. Two peptide-forming condensations remove 2×18=36, leaving 233 g/mol. The alternatives subtract zero, one or three waters. This calculation uses the supplied rounded free masses, not an already residue-based table.

question: An oriented four-residue peptide permits any of twenty residues independently at each position, including repetition. How many sequences are possible?
explanation: The multiplication rule gives 20×20×20×20=20^4=160,000. Eighty adds rather than multiplies choices; 24 applies to four distinct fixed residues without repetition; 116,280 counts 20×19×18×17 arrangements without repetition, contrary to the stated independent choices.

question: A peptide has exactly two glycines and one alanine. How many distinguishable N→C orders are possible?
options: Twenty-seven
Three
One
Six
explanation: The distinguishable orders are GGA, GAG and AGG, or 3!/2!=3. One ignores order; six treats the two glycines as distinguishable. Twenty-seven assumes three independent distinguishable choices at each position and fails the fixed-composition condition.

question: Complete ideal hydrolysis gives equal Gly/Ala/Ser composition for two different tripeptides. What remains unresolved from composition alone?
options: The identities of all three detected residue types
The reported total number of detected residues under the ideal assumptions
The original N→C order of those residues
Whether any amino-acid residues were present
explanation: Composition counts residue types but erases their original order. Detecting the stated identities and totals does not recover the sequence; overlapping fragments or another sequencing method are needed. This limitation differs from uncertain analytical recovery, which adds a further problem.

question: Strong-acid analysis reports ten Asx residues and no tryptophan peak. Which interpretation is justified?
options: The original protein necessarily contained ten Asp and zero Asn.
The missing tryptophan peak proves the original protein lacked tryptophan.
The analysis uniquely identifies the complete original sequence.
Asx combines original Asp/Asn, and acid destruction can explain an absent tryptophan signal.
explanation: Asparagine can be converted into aspartate, making Asx a combined category; tryptophan is destroyed under ordinary acid-hydrolysis conditions. Therefore neither the exact original Asp count nor tryptophan absence is proven, and composition cannot establish sequence.

question: Which pair describes the characteristic hydrogen bond of a regular α helix?
options: Backbone carbonyl O of residue i and backbone N–H of residue i+4
Side-chain carbon of i and side-chain carbon of i+1
A covalent peptide bond directly from i to i+4
Two sulphur atoms on every fourth residue
explanation: The regular α-helix pattern is a backbone hydrogen bond from C=O at i to N–H at i+4. Peptide covalent links still connect successive residues. The pattern neither requires paired sulfurs nor represents a direct side-chain carbon bond.

question: For an ideal uninterrupted twenty-residue α-helical segment, how many internal i→i+4 hydrogen bonds fit entirely within the segment?
options: Five
Sixteen
Twenty
Nineteen
explanation: The donor/acceptor index pairs start at i=1 and end at i=16, where i+4=20, giving 20−4=16. Nineteen counts linear peptide bonds, twenty ignores end limitations and five divides residue count by four rather than counting eligible pairs.

question: Using an explicitly supplied ideal α-helical rise of 0.15 nm per residue, estimate the axial length for twenty residues.
options: 30 nm
133 nm
3.0 nm
explanation: The ideal estimate is 20×0.15=3.0 nm. The other values reflect factor-of-ten or inverted-unit errors. This model gives an approximate helix-axis length rather than an actual measured structure or a fully extended chain length.

question: Two neighbouring β strands run in opposite N→C directions. What is this arrangement?
options: Parallel
An α-helix i+4 covalent linkage
A disulfide-only chain reversal
Antiparallel
explanation: Opposing sequence directions define an antiparallel sheet arrangement; matching directions define parallel. Interstrand backbone hydrogen bonding differs from the helical i+4 pattern. A disulfide is a different covalent side-chain connection and does not define strand direction.

question: Which feature helps explain collagen triple-helix packing?
options: Glycine occurs at every third position in the characteristic Gly–X–Y repeat.
Each collagen chain must be an ordinary right-handed α helix.
Every third residue must have the bulkiest available side chain.
The triple helix is a single polypeptide with three domains only.
explanation: Small glycine side chains permit tight packing in the characteristic triple-chain structure. Collagen is not simply three ordinary α helices, and a bulky replacement can interfere with the required geometry. Three chains are distinct from three domains of one chain.

question: A single polypeptide contains two compact domains. What can be concluded from that fact alone?
options: Each domain must be a separate N→C backbone.
It can remain monomeric; two domains do not imply two polypeptide chains.
It must be a heterodimer.
It must contain no tertiary structure.
explanation: Domains are regions within a chain, whereas a dimer contains two subunits. A multidomain chain still has a tertiary arrangement. Independent backbones and heterodimeric composition require additional evidence rather than counting compact regions.

question: What best explains a common contribution of nonpolar side-chain burial to soluble-protein folding?
options: Water is absent from all surfaces of soluble proteins.
Only disulfides can stabilise a folded chain.
Reducing nonpolar surface exposed to water can favour the folded arrangement through the hydrophobic effect.
Every hydrophobic contact creates a new covalent peptide bond.
explanation: The hydrophobic effect involves solvent consequences of nonpolar exposure, not a new covalent bond. Water remains around soluble proteins, and packing, hydrogen bonds, electrostatics and sometimes disulfides also contribute. Net stability depends on combined favourable effects and costs.

question: Which arrangement is plausible for a membrane channel?
options: A uniformly nonpolar surface including every water-exposed pore position
No hydrophobic residues anywhere in its membrane-spanning region
An exclusively soluble globular protein with no membrane interaction
Hydrophobic lipid-facing surfaces with polar groups lining an aqueous pathway
explanation: Different surfaces contact different environments. Lipid-facing regions often expose hydrophobic groups while a water-accessible pore can present polar groups. A membrane protein need not be uniformly hydrophobic, but membrane-spanning regions cannot be explained by ignoring lipid interactions.

question: A hypothetical enzyme loses activity in urea and regains it after urea removal while its peptide sequence remains unchanged. What is the best supported interpretation?
options: Reversible disruption and restoration of a functional fold
Complete peptide hydrolysis followed by spontaneous resynthesis
Replacement of every side chain by urea
Proof that every enzyme always refolds without assistance
explanation: The observations are consistent with reversible denaturation/refolding without changing sequence. Hydrolysis/resynthesis would require additional covalent evidence and chemistry. One protein’s recovery does not establish universal refolding, and urea exposure does not mean all side chains were replaced.

question: In a typical α2β2 assembly, α and β denote distinct polypeptide types. How many chains and types are present?
options: Two α helices and two β sheets with no chain information
Four chains and two types
Two chains and four types
Four chains and four necessarily different types
explanation: Subscripts count copies of each chain type: two α plus two β gives four chains of two types. These labels do not specify secondary structures. Counting the symbols alone misses the repeated copies, while counting each copy as a new type confuses identity with multiplicity.

question: Which comparison between typical haemoglobin A and myoglobin is correct?
options: Myoglobin has four identical oxygen-binding chains.
Haem binding proves the proteins have identical physiological roles.
Haemoglobin has multiple interacting oxygen-binding subunits; myoglobin is a one-chain protein with one oxygen-binding site.
Both necessarily have α2β2 composition.
explanation: Haemoglobin’s assembly supports communication between its sites, while single-chain myoglobin lacks that same multi-site organisation. Both use haem but differ in organisation and role. A common prosthetic group does not force identical chain counts or functions.

question: What does positive oxygen-binding cooperativity in haemoglobin mean?
options: The first oxygen creates extra polypeptide chains.
Every site must always be occupied together.
Bound oxygen is necessarily consumed as a chemical substrate.
Binding can favour conformational states with higher affinity at remaining sites.
explanation: Cooperativity concerns linked binding equilibria and conformational populations. It does not change the number of subunits or require all-or-none permanent occupancy. Reversible oxygen binding differs from consuming oxygen in a catalytic reaction.

question: A hypothetical α2β2 protein has 100 residues per α chain and 80 per β chain. How many ordinary backbone peptide bonds are present in the four separate linear chains?
explanation: Total residues are 2×100+2×80=360. Subtract one terminal gap per separate chain: 360−4=356. Subtracting one treats all chains as continuous; 360 counts residues; 352 incorrectly subtracts twice per chain. Noncovalent association adds no peptide bonds.

question: In the haemoglobin example, why can replacing glutamate with valine affect intermolecular association?
options: It makes all mutant molecules permanently unfolded regardless of conditions.
It replaces a usually charged side chain with a hydrophobic one, changing surface interactions.
It automatically removes every peptide bond from the β chain.
It converts haem into a carbohydrate.
explanation: The substitution changes local chemistry and can favour abnormal association of deoxygenated HbS molecules. This is different from wholesale hydrolysis, a change of haem class or universal permanent unfolding. The structural mechanism must be interpreted in its molecular and clinical context.

question: Why is a phosphotyrosine residue alone insufficient to guarantee binding by any SH2-containing protein?
options: Every phosphorylated residue is a proline-rich sequence.
SH2 binding necessarily hydrolyses every peptide bond.
Recognition also depends on the surrounding motif and appropriate molecular context.
SH2 domains recognise only peptide length and never chemistry.
explanation: SH2 domains commonly recognise suitable phosphotyrosine-containing motifs, so context and accessibility matter. SH3 domains have different common recognition preferences. Binding is a selective interaction, not automatic destruction of the protein backbone.

question: Which statement about haemoprotein and metalloprotein categories is correct?
options: Every metal-containing protein must have haem.
Haemoprotein describes only a protein’s chain number.
A protein cannot simultaneously be an enzyme and a haemoprotein.
Haemoproteins are metalloproteins, but other metalloproteins need not contain haem.
explanation: Haem contains iron in a particular porphyrin group, making haemoproteins a subset of metal-containing proteins. Other metal associations exist. Chemical composition, subunit number and physiological function are different classification axes, so an enzyme can also be a haemoprotein.

question: Which functional pairing is correct?
options: Ferritin — iron storage
Albumin — only DNA sequence replication
Insulin — a steroid made of fused hydrocarbon rings
Tubulin — the same ATP-driven motor as myosin
explanation: Ferritin stores iron. Albumin transports several substances, insulin is a peptide/protein hormone and tubulin builds microtubules rather than being interchangeable with myosin. Related or overlapping cellular roles do not make these molecules chemically or mechanistically identical.

question: What distinguishes a prosthetic group from an arbitrary substrate transiently contacting a protein?
options: It must always be covalently linked and can never be noncovalent.
It is a tightly associated nonprotein component important to the protein’s function; covalent attachment is not required.
It must be another complete polypeptide subunit.
It is necessarily every molecule present in the same solution.
explanation: A prosthetic group is an integral, tightly associated functional component; linkage can be covalent or noncovalent. An ordinary substrate may bind and leave during turnover without becoming a prosthetic group. A complete polypeptide partner is a different structural category.

question: In ordinary size-exclusion chromatography within the useful fractionation range, why do larger molecules often elute earlier?
options: They must carry a more positive net charge.
They pass through more pore volume than all smaller molecules.
They access less internal bead-pore volume.
They bind most strongly to an immobilised affinity ligand.
explanation: Larger molecules explore less internal pore space and take a shorter accessible path. This size-based mechanism differs from affinity binding or ion exchange. Shape, aggregation and column range affect interpretation; early elution alone does not establish molecular identity.

question: Which ion-exchanger description is correct?
options: A cation exchanger has fixed positive groups and binds anions.
An anion exchanger has no charge-bearing groups.
The resin charge must always equal the retained solute charge.
A cation exchanger has fixed negative groups and can bind positively charged solutes.
explanation: The name refers to the exchanged solute: negatively charged resin retains cations, while positively charged resin retains anions. Opposite charges favour interaction under suitable conditions. Actual retention also depends on buffer, salt and surface properties.

question: A hypothetical protein has pI 8 and is placed in a pH 6 buffer. Which charge-based prediction is plausible?
options: It tends net positive and may bind a suitable cation exchanger.
It tends net negative because pH is below pI.
It must have zero charge because pI and pH are both numbers.
Its charge proves its exact amino-acid sequence.
explanation: Below pI the average net charge tends positive, supporting possible binding to a negative cation-exchange resin. Above pI the tendency reverses. This is a conditional prediction rather than guaranteed retention or sequence determination.

question: A multimer gives smaller polypeptide bands after SDS treatment and reduction. What inference avoids conflating distinct processes?
options: One visible band establishes exact sequence identity by itself.
Subunit association and disulfides can be disrupted without deliberate peptide-backbone hydrolysis.
Every smaller band proves that every peptide bond was cleaved.
SDS-PAGE directly proves native activity of each band.
explanation: SDS can unfold/dissociate complexes and a reducing reagent cleaves susceptible disulfides, allowing intact individual chains to separate. Peptide cleavage is a different reaction. Band appearance supports size/heterogeneity analysis but does not alone prove sequence identity or retained native function.

question: An extract has 100 mg total protein and 200 activity units; a fraction has 10 mg and 100 units. What are its enrichment and activity recovery?
options: Twofold enrichment and 10% recovery
Fivefold enrichment and 5% recovery
Fivefold enrichment and 50% recovery
Tenfold enrichment and 100% recovery
explanation: Initial specific activity=200/100=2 units/mg; final=100/10=10 units/mg, so enrichment=10/2=5. Activity recovery=100/200×100=50%. Total mass reduction alone is not the activity recovery or purification factor.

question: Which interpretation of salting out best retains the source’s useful principle without imposing a universal threshold?
options: Every protein precipitates irreversibly above exactly 1 M of every salt.
Salt precipitation always proves peptide-bond hydrolysis.
Low and high salt must have identical effects on every protein.
Suitable high salt can decrease solubility, but protein, ion identity, pH and temperature determine the conditions.
explanation: Salting-in and salting-out are condition-dependent solubility behaviours. The lecture’s molarity divisions illustrate trends, not universal constants. Precipitation can be reversible and does not by itself demonstrate denaturation or backbone cleavage.

question: A reaction is thermodynamically favourable but slow under the stated conditions. What can explain this?
options: A substantial activation barrier can limit rate despite a favourable reaction free-energy change.
Negative ΔG means there can be no activation barrier.
A slow rate proves the reaction equilibrium favours only reactants.
Thermodynamic driving force and reaction rate are identical quantities.
explanation: ΔG compares initial and final states, while ΔG‡ concerns a barrier along the pathway. A favourable endpoint does not remove that barrier or specify rate. Slow reaction alone cannot determine the equilibrium composition, so kinetic and thermodynamic evidence must be kept distinct.

question: For the same reactant and product states, what does an enzyme alone change?
options: The identity of atoms required by the balanced reaction
The accessible catalytic pathway and rate of approach to equilibrium
The equilibrium constant of the isolated reaction
The net reaction free-energy difference by supplying unlimited energy
explanation: An enzyme lowers relevant pathway barriers while preserving the free-energy difference and equilibrium constant for the same states. It does not supply unlimited free energy or change atom conservation. Coupling another reaction can alter the overall process, but is a separate thermodynamic intervention.

question: At equilibrium in an enzyme-catalysed reversible reaction, which statement is appropriate?
options: Product can no longer bind any enzyme.
Only the forward reaction continues with a positive net rate.
Forward and reverse molecular reaction rates can be equal and nonzero.
Every enzyme molecule must be irreversibly inactive.
explanation: Equilibrium is dynamic: equal opposing rates yield no net change. It does not require enzyme destruction or loss of product binding. A continuing unequal forward flux would instead imply that equilibrium has not been reached or that the system is maintained away from it.

question: Comparable first-order constants are 3×10^4 s−1 catalysed and 3×10−10 s−1 uncatalysed. What dimensionless rate ratio follows?
explanation: Divide like constants: (3/3)×10^(4−(−10))=10^14, with s−1 cancelling. Reversing the ratio gives 10−14; adding exponents or multiplying prefactors does not compute the requested quotient. This ratio does not describe a change in reaction ΔG.

question: Why can residues distant in a protein’s sequence contribute to one active site?
options: Folding can place their chemical groups near one another in three dimensions.
Only adjacent residues can interact in any protein.
Active sites are always separate free amino-acid molecules.
A peptide sequence contains no spatial information or constraints.
explanation: Tertiary folding brings selected distant positions together, allowing a coordinated binding/catalytic environment. Adjacency in primary sequence is not required. The site is part of the organised protein, whose sequence and environment constrain the possible fold.

question: What limitation does induced fit address in a rigid lock-and-key analogy?
options: Every ligand must bind without affecting any molecular interaction.
Ligand-associated conformational changes can improve productive alignment.
Enzymes never recognise chemical structure.
Substrate binding must permanently destroy the protein.
explanation: Induced fit incorporates conformational changes associated with recognition and catalysis. It retains selective chemical interactions rather than denying recognition. These changes can be reversible and productive; they do not imply permanent destruction or absence of molecular effects.

question: A catalytic residue temporarily forms an enzyme-linked intermediate and is regenerated after product release. What strategy is illustrated?
options: A permanent loss of all catalytic centres
Only a thermodynamic change in equilibrium constant
Covalent catalysis
Necessarily irreversible poisoning
explanation: A temporary productive covalent intermediate is covalent catalysis. Regeneration distinguishes that cycle from persistent disabling modification. Its existence neither requires loss of every active centre nor means the enzyme changes the equilibrium constant of the overall reaction.

question: Analogue A binds tightly but gives no product, while substrate B undergoes repeated turnover. Which conclusion is supported?
options: A must have the highest catalytic rate because its binding is strongest.
B cannot be a substrate unless it binds more tightly than A.
Any strongly bound molecule must become product at equilibrium.
Binding strength alone does not establish that A is the better substrate.
explanation: A may bind without productive alignment or may inhibit. Substrate performance requires transformation rates and relevant kinetic conditions, not binding alone. Productive turnover and tight ground-state binding are different observations; neither imposes the asserted universal affinity ranking.

question: What does an EC identifier primarily classify?
options: An enzymatic catalytic activity by its reaction
One unique gene accession in one organism
The number of polypeptide chains in every enzyme molecule
A universal optimum temperature
explanation: EC nomenclature is reaction based. Different sequences can catalyse the same classified activity, and one protein can carry several activities. Chain number, temperature and gene identity require separate information rather than being read from an EC code.

question: Which class is supported for an activity that hydrolyses a peptide linkage using water?
options: EC 7 translocase
EC 3 hydrolase
EC 2 transferase
EC 5 isomerase
explanation: Hydrolytic peptide cleavage is a hydrolase activity. A transferase moves a group between partners, an isomerase rearranges connectivity within the corresponding molecular formula and a translocase concerns a classified coupled movement process. The water-assisted bond-cleavage chemistry decides this example.

question: ATP transfers a phosphoryl group to a sugar hydroxyl, producing ADP and a phosphorylated sugar. Which broad activity class is indicated?
options: Isomerase because the sugar remains present
Translocase because phosphate is charged
Transferase
Hydrolase merely because ATP is involved
explanation: This kinase-type activity transfers a phosphoryl group from ATP to an acceptor. ATP participation alone does not make every activity a hydrolase. Neither an unchanged molecular formula nor a membrane-translocation event is described. Classification follows the complete reaction.

question: Why can a hydratase adding water across a double bond be classed as a lyase rather than a hydrolase?
options: Every reaction involving water must be EC 3.
A lyase must oxidise NADH in every reaction.
Water addition necessarily creates an ATP-dependent ligase reaction.
Addition across the double bond differs from hydrolytic cleavage of the substrate.
explanation: Lyase-type reversible addition/elimination chemistry differs from hydrolysis even when water participates. Water, NADH or ATP names alone do not define a class. Identify what bonds are formed or broken and the full coupled reaction.

question: Which statement correctly qualifies EC 7 translocases?
options: The classified activity considers coupled translocation, so a generic reductase name alone is insufficient.
Every protein that binds a quinone is automatically EC 7.
Every passive membrane pore must have an EC 7 catalytic activity.
The current nomenclature omits translocases and has only six classes.
explanation: EC 7 is present in the source and current nomenclature, with subclasses linked to specified driving reactions and transported species. A generic reductase label or passive pore does not establish the required complete coupled activity. Classification needs the actual reaction description.

question: Which statement distinguishes a required cofactor from the apoenzyme?
options: All cofactors are permanently covalently bound vitamins.
The apoenzyme is the protein component without its required cofactor.
A cofactor is always a second full polypeptide chain.
Every apoenzyme must retain full catalytic function without its required partner.
